title: Towards Evaluating the Robustness of Neural Networks
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2017 (arXiv:1608.04644)

pages.title: How strong is the strongest attack?
pages.subtitle: Building attacks to honestly measure robustness

blocks.html: A defense is only as convincing as the attack it survives. If you test a model against a weak attack and it holds up, you have learned almost nothing. This paper sets out to build the strongest possible attacks, so that surviving them is real evidence of robustness.

The immediate target is defensive distillation, a method that had been reported to reduce the success rate of existing attacks from 95% down to 0.5% and was held up as a strong defense. The authors construct three new attacks, one for each of the $\ell_2$, $\ell_0$, and $\ell_\infty$ distance metrics, and show that defensive distillation provides essentially no protection against them: their attacks succeed 100% of the time on both the original and the distilled network.

The lasting contribution is not just breaking one defense. It is a careful, optimization-based methodology for crafting minimal-distortion adversarial examples that became the de facto benchmark for evaluating every defense that came after.
We do not propose a defense; we propose attacks powerful enough that defeating them is meaningful.

pages.title: Adversarial examples as constrained optimization
pages.subtitle: Find the smallest change that flips the label

blocks.html: The cleanest way to state the goal is as a constrained optimization: among all perturbations $\delta$ that cause the model to output a chosen target class $t$, find the one with the smallest size under a distance metric $D$ (such as $\ell_2$).

blocks.tex: \min_{\delta} \; D(x, x+\delta) \quad \text{such that} \quad C(x+\delta) = t \;,\; x+\delta \in [0,1]^n

blocks.html: In words: minimize the distortion $D$ between the clean image $x$ and the adversarial image $x+\delta$, subject to two constraints, that the classifier $C$ assigns the target label $t$, and that the result stays a valid image with every pixel in $[0,1]$.

This is hard to optimize directly because the constraint $C(x+\delta)=t$ is highly non-linear and non-differentiable (it depends on an argmax over logits). The bulk of the paper is a sequence of design choices that turn this awkward problem into one that a gradient-based optimizer can solve well.

pages.title: Moving the constraint into the objective
pages.subtitle: A differentiable surrogate for 'is misclassified'

blocks.html: The first move is to relax the hard classification constraint into a soft penalty. Instead of requiring $C(x+\delta)=t$ exactly, the authors add a term $f(x+\delta)$ that is non-positive precisely when the image is classified as the target, and minimize a weighted sum.

Reading this: minimize the size of the perturbation plus a constant $c$ times a surrogate $f$ that measures how far the image is from being misclassified as $t$. The constant $c$ trades off the two goals; the authors find a good $c$ by binary search, the smallest value that still yields a successful attack, which keeps the distortion minimal.

The choice of $f$ matters. After testing several candidates, the most effective surrogate works on the logits $Z$ rather than the softmax probabilities, comparing the target logit against the strongest competing logit:

In words: $f$ is the gap between the best non-target logit and the target logit. When the target already wins, the gap is negative and $f$ stops pushing once it reaches $-\kappa$. The parameter $\kappa$ is a confidence margin: larger $\kappa$ forces the adversarial example deeper into the target region, which makes the attack transfer better to other models at the cost of more distortion.

The second constraint, that every pixel stays in $[0,1]$, is usually handled by clipping after each gradient step. Clipping wastes optimizer effort: the gradient may keep pushing a pixel past the boundary while clipping silently throws that work away. Carlini and Wagner instead remove the box constraint entirely with a change of variables.

Read this as: optimize over an unconstrained variable $w$, and map it through $\tanh$ (squashed to $[0,1]$) to get the actual pixel value $x'$. Because $\tanh$ smoothly saturates, every value of $w$ produces a valid image automatically, and the optimizer can use a strong method like Adam over $w$ with no clipping at all. This change of variables is a large part of why the attack finds such small perturbations.

items: Surrogate $f$ on logits, not probabilities, to avoid the vanishing gradients distillation creates.
Binary search over $c$ to find the minimum-distortion success.
tanh reparameterization to satisfy the box constraint smoothly.
Adam as the inner optimizer, run for many iterations per example.

blocks.html: Different threat models care about different notions of a small change, so the paper builds an attack for each of three metrics, all sharing the same surrogate and tanh tricks.

rows: Total squared change across all pixels
Spreads a faint, smooth perturbation over the whole image; the flagship attack.
Number of pixels changed at all
Iteratively fixes unimportant pixels and changes only a small critical set.
Largest change to any single pixel
Caps every pixel's change; uses a penalty on the max to avoid the non-differentiable corner.

blocks.html: The $\ell_0$ attack is built on top of the $\ell_2$ attack: it repeatedly runs the $\ell_2$ attack and freezes the pixels that matter least, shrinking the set of modified pixels. The $\ell_\infty$ attack replaces the hard max (whose gradient only touches one pixel at a time) with a smoother penalty that pushes down all pixels exceeding a shrinking threshold $\tau$.

Across all three metrics, the attacks find adversarial examples with distortions far smaller than previous methods such as FGSM or the earlier L-BFGS attack, often producing changes that are visually undetectable.

Defensive distillation works by training a second network on the soft probability outputs of a first, using a high softmax temperature. This flattens the gradients an attacker sees, so gradient-based attacks struggle, the source of the celebrated drop to a 0.5% attack success rate.

The C&W attacks defeat this by operating on the logits rather than the softmax outputs, sidestepping the flattened probabilities entirely. The result is decisive: the attacks succeed 100% of the time on both undistilled and distilled networks across MNIST and CIFAR, and distillation increases the required distortion only marginally.

The lesson generalizes beyond distillation: a defense that merely hides or flattens gradients can look extremely robust against weak attacks while offering no real protection. Honest evaluation requires attacks that adapt to the defense, a theme the obfuscated-gradients work would formalize a year later.

pages.title: Why this became the benchmark
pages.subtitle: Strong attacks as a measuring instrument

items: It established that minimum-distortion attacks, not one-shot attacks, are the right yardstick for robustness.
The logit-based surrogate, binary search over $c$, and tanh reparameterization became standard tools.
The confidence parameter $\kappa$ gave a knob for trading distortion against transferability, useful for black-box attacks.
The C&W $\ell_2$ attack became the default sanity check: a defense that does not survive it is not considered robust.

blocks.html: By demonstrating that a celebrated defense collapsed completely under a properly designed attack, the paper changed the standard of evidence in the field. From then on, claiming robustness meant surviving strong, adaptive, optimization-based attacks, and C&W was the attack everyone reached for first.
If your defense has only been tested against weak attacks, you have not tested it at all.
